title: Arm Squeeze Test
purpose: Differentiate referred arm pain from cervical root compression versus shoulder pathology.
structure: Superficial radial, ulnar and median nerves in the middle third of the upper arm, sensitised by compression of a cervical root C5-T1.
procedure: Patient sitting; stand behind the affected shoulder. Grasp the middle third of the arm with the thumb over the triceps and four fingers over the biceps and squeeze three times with equal pressure. For comparison apply digital pressure to the acromioclavicular joint and the anterolateral subacromial area. Patient rates pain at each of the three sites on a VAS.
positive: Arm-squeeze pain at least 3 points higher than at the other two sites.

accuracy.source: Gumina et al. 2013 (Eur Spine J), over 1200 patients

notes: Hypothesis: squeezing compresses skin, subcutis and muscle onto the nerves, which are painful when a cervical root is pathologically compressed but not in shoulder pathology.

title: Neck Tornado Test
purpose: New provocation test for cervical radiculopathy (Choi's test) applying compression at all angles.
procedure: Patient sitting, fixated with one hand; stand behind and apply light pressure to the vertex. With constant pressure, rotate the neck in a 180-degree tornadic pattern: maximal flexion, then lateral bending and full extension towards the painful side.
positive: Reproduction or aggravation of radicular pain or tingling in the ipsilateral shoulder or upper extremity.

accuracy.source: Park et al. (text 2019, reference 2017, Int J Med Sci), compared with Spurling's test

notes: Source: questionable clinical value for now (high risk of bias, no follow-up studies). Whether ipsilateral shoulder pain should count is questionable (could be facet-referred). ⚠ Park cited as 2019 in text, 2017 in the reference list. Radiculopathy: 75% from foraminal narrowing by spondylosis, 25% from posterolateral disc herniation (under 50 years).

title: Dermatomes Upper Limb
purpose: Dermatome testing as part of the peripheral neurological examination for cervical radiculopathy, to identify the pathological disc level.
structure: Cervical dermatomes of the upper limb. Most common levels C5-6 and C6-7; herniated (soft) discs 20-25%, degenerative (hard) disc disease 70-75%.
procedure: Patient recumbent with both arms exposed. Stroke the dermatomal regions with a brush (e.g. from the reflex hammer handle) on affected and unaffected limb and ask for side-to-side differences; also brush across dermatomes on the same side.
positive: Altered sensation in a dermatome compared with the other side or adjacent dermatomes.

accuracy.source: Lemeunier et al. 2017 CADRE systematic review (Eur Spine J); Wainner 2003 also listed

notes: Source: rather weak clinical value, but the best tool available. Companion pages: myotomes and reflexes upper limb; lower-limb neurological examination (lumbar region).

title: Myotomes Upper Limb
purpose: Myotome strength testing as part of the peripheral neurological examination for cervical radiculopathy.
structure: C4/5 deltoid; C5/6 biceps and wrist extensors; C6/7 triceps and wrist flexors; C7/8 abductor pollicis; T1 dorsal interossei.
procedure: Patient sitting; compare sides. Deltoid: arms abducted about 90 degrees, press down. Biceps: forearm flexed 90 degrees, resist your extension force. Wrist extensors: pronated forearm on the table, fist in slight extension, apply a flexion force. Triceps: forearm flexed 90 degrees, resist your flexion force. Wrist flexors: supinated forearm, fist in slight flexion, apply an extension force. Abductor pollicis brevis: supinated forearm, open hand, patient resists (page: 'thumb adduction'). Dorsal interossei: interlock fingers, patient squeezes.

accuracy.sensitivity: deltoid 24%; biceps 24%; wrist extensors 12%; triceps 12%; wrist flexors 6%; abductor pollicis 6%; dorsal interosseous 3%; complete examination 83%
accuracy.specificity: deltoid 89%; biceps 94%; wrist extensors 90%; triceps 94%; wrist flexors 89%; abductor pollicis 84%; dorsal interosseous 93%; complete examination 28%
accuracy.source: per-muscle values from Wainner et al. 2003 as listed on the page; complete examination from Lemeunier et al. 2017 (CADRE)

notes: Source: rather weak clinical value but the best tool available. ⚠ For abductor pollicis brevis the page says 'ask the patient to resist thumb adduction', i.e. the examiner pushes the thumb into adduction while the patient abducts.

title: Reflex Testing Upper Limb
purpose: Deep tendon reflex testing as part of the peripheral neurological examination for cervical radiculopathy.
structure: Biceps tendon reflex (C5, C6); triceps tendon reflex (C7).
procedure: Biceps: patient recumbent, forearm slightly flexed, palpate the biceps tendon and tap briskly with the reflex hammer. Triceps: arm slightly abducted with the relaxed forearm hanging; tap the tendon just proximal to the olecranon. Grade 0 (no response, always abnormal), 1+ (slight), 2+ (brisk, usually normal), 3+ (very brisk), 4+ (clonus, always abnormal).
positive: Diminished/absent (0, 1+) or exaggerated (3+, 4+) reflex compared with the other side.

accuracy.source: biceps reflex values as listed on the page (Wainner 2003 data); complete examination Lemeunier et al. 2017 (CADRE)

notes: Source: rather weak clinical value but still the best tool available. No accuracy figure is given for the triceps reflex. The page's 'other parts' list repeats 'Reflex Testing (Lower Limb)' under the upper-limb heading.

title: Cervical Spondylotic Myelopathy Cluster
purpose: Cluster of clinical findings (Cook et al. 2010) to detect or rule out cervical spondylotic myelopathy (CSM).
structure: Cervical spinal cord compression; the most common cause of atraumatic spinal cord injury in the elderly.
procedure: Five findings: (1) gait deviation (wide-based, ataxic or spastic); (2) positive Hoffmann's sign; (3) inverted supinator sign; (4) positive Babinski sign; (5) age over 45 years.
positive: 3 of 5 positive strongly suggests CSM; only 1 of 5 positive helps rule it out.

accuracy.source: Cook et al. 2010 (J Man Manip Ther), clinical diagnosis as reference standard

notes: Symptoms: gait abnormality, weak or stiff legs of insidious onset, clumsy hands, reduced hand sensation; central cord signs such as spasticity and urinary retention. Hoffmann, inverted supinator and Babinski pages are in the screening region.

title: Lhermitte’s Sign
purpose: Sign of dorsal column / spinal cord involvement (multiple sclerosis, cervical myelopathy, spondylosis, trauma).
structure: Dorsal column of the spinal cord; hyperexcitable demyelinated nerves or cord compression/stretch.
procedure: Patient standing or sitting flexes the neck.
positive: An electric-shock or pins-and-needles sensation down the spine, possibly into the extremities, near end-range flexion.
notes: Source: evidence sparse and rates the sign poorly. Other UMN screens: Babinski, inverted supinator, Hoffmann (screening region). Source files this page under 'Neurological Assessment'.

title: Clinical Cervical Instability
purpose: Delphi-derived subjective and objective identifiers of clinical cervical spine instability / cervical motor control impairment (Cook et al. 2005).
procedure: Top 5 subjective: intolerance to prolonged static postures; fatigue and inability to hold the head up; symptom decrease with external support (propping on hands, collar); frequent need for self-manipulation; feeling of instability, shaking or lack of control. Top 5 objective: poor coordination/neuromuscular control (poor recruitment, dissociation of segments); abnormal joint play; motion not smooth through range (hinging, pivoting, fulcruming); aberrant movement; hypomobility of the upper thoracic spine.
positive: Not a single test; a pattern of these identifiers suggests clinical instability.

accuracy.source: n/a; Delphi study (Cook et al. 2005, Phys Ther) because no valid clinical test for spinal instability exists

notes: Companion tests: craniocervical flexion test, deep neck flexor endurance test, cervical extensor endurance test. Lumbar counterpart in the lumbar region.

title: Craniocervical Flexion Test
purpose: Test deep cervical flexor activation and isometric endurance (CCFT) with a pressure biofeedback unit; deficits are associated with neck pain and cervicogenic headache.
structure: Deep cervical flexors (longus colli/capitis) versus superficial sternocleidomastoid and anterior scalenes.
procedure: Patient supine crook-lying, head neutral, face horizontal; deflated biofeedback cuff behind the neck against the occiput, inflated to 20 mmHg. Stage 1: slow head nod (back of the head slides up the bench) to raise pressure 2 mmHg (22), hold 2-3 s, relax; repeat in 2 mmHg steps to 30 mmHg (5 stages); nod on exhalation if apical breathing. Watch for increasing nod angle, no head retraction or lifting, minimal palpable SCM/scalene activity until the last 1-2 stages, return to 20 mmHg between attempts. Stage 2 (if stage 1 is clean): hold the nod at 22 mmHg for 10 s; three 10-second holds allow progression by 2 mmHg; watch for jerkiness or pressure loss.
positive: Record the highest stage achieved with correct craniocervical flexion (stage 1) and the pressure level held steadily for repeated 10-second holds with minimal superficial activity (stage 2).

accuracy.source: n/a (performance test). Reliability: de Koning et al. 2008 systematic review, intra-observer ICC 0.65-0.93, inter-observer ICC 0.54 (one study); Jull et al. 2008 protocol

notes: Source: rather weak clinical value because of inconsistent reliability results. Companion tests: deep neck flexor endurance (test of Harris), cervical extensor endurance, clinical cervical instability.

title: Deep Neck Flexor Endurance Test
purpose: Timed endurance test of the deep neck flexors in neck pain or headache (also called test of Harris).
procedure: Patient supine hook-lying, chin maximally retracted; lift the head and neck about 2.5 cm (1 inch) off the table keeping the chin tucked. Time the hold; keep one hand on the table under the occiput. Cue when the chin skin folds separate or the occiput touches your hand; stop when the chin tuck is lost or the occiput rests on your hand for more than 1 second.
positive: Hold time compared with normative data: mean 39 s for men and 29 s for women (126 asymptomatic adults aged 20-80).

accuracy.source: n/a (performance test). Normative data Domenech et al. (text 2015, reference 2011, PM&R); inter-rater reliability reported as 66%

notes: ⚠ Domenech cited as 2015 in text, 2011 in the reference list. Companion tests: craniocervical flexion test, cervical extensor endurance test, clinical cervical instability.

title: Cervical Extensor Endurance Test
purpose: Identify weakness of the deep and superficial neck extensors (CEET).
procedure: Patient prone with head and neck beyond the edge of the table and the cervicothoracic junction stabilised; patient sustains a chin-tuck in neutral for 20 seconds, observed with an inclinometer or by eye.
positive: Deep extensor weakness: chin length increases with neck extension (superficial dominance), a change of 5-10 degrees from maximal craniocervical flexion towards relative extension. Global weakness: the head drops into flexion, a flexion deflection of more than 10 degrees.

accuracy.source: n/a (performance test). Sebastian et al. 2015 reliability study (J Bodyw Mov Ther)

notes: An inclinometer gives objective values but may not be needed in routine practice. Companion tests: deep neck flexor endurance, craniocervical flexion, clinical cervical instability.

title: Flexion Rotation Test
purpose: Identify upper cervical (C1/2) rotation impairment, especially in cervicogenic headache.
structure: Atlanto-axial (C1/2) rotation with the lower cervical spine locked in flexion.
procedure: Patient supine; bring the cervical spine into maximal flexion, then rotate the head left and right to end-range (pain or firm resistance). Healthy average about 44 degrees per side.
positive: A visually estimated reduction of 10 degrees or more from the expected 44 degrees (slightly more than the minimal detectable change).

accuracy.source: Ogince et al. 2007 (Man Ther), C1/2-related cervicogenic headache; reliability Hall et al. 2010, intra-rater 0.95-0.97, MDC 7 degrees

notes: A positive test does not say which upper cervical segment is hypomobile; segmental PIVM assessment is needed (page links to a blog on upper cervical PIVMs).
